findings.headline: The council's £6m commercial property fund investment has fallen to £5.470m, a loss of £530k reflecting UK property market decline.
findings.detail: Mid Sussex holds £5.470m in the Local Authorities' Property Fund as of 31 March 2026, down from £6m invested. The report explicitly attributes this to the general decline in commercial property prices in the UK. The council has set aside a provision in reserves against the risk of this decline relating to the IFRS9 statutory override, which extends only to March 2029. The fund generated £255k dividend income in 2025/26.
findings.matters: A significant unrealised loss on a pooled investment fund indicates exposure to commercial property market risk. The need to provision against further potential losses directly impacts the council's reserves and balance sheet strength, which lenders consider when assessing creditworthiness and capacity to manage financial shocks.
findings.figures: £5.470m current value (from £6m invested); £530k loss; £255k dividend income in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Fund was valued at 31 March 2026 at £5.470m. This reflects the general decline in commercial property prices in the UK. A provision has been set aside in reserves for any risk of this decline relating to the IFRS9 statutory override ending

findings.headline: Abandoned vehicles service performance deteriorated from 97% to 62% resolution rate, expected to continue into 2026/27
findings.detail: The percentage of abandoned vehicles cases resolved within seven days has declined throughout the year from 97% in Q1 to 62% in Q4 due to delay in a system change used county-wide with Sussex Police and the County Council. The service has flagged that this slippage may continue to be a challenge in the first half of 2026/27.
findings.matters: Significant operational performance deterioration flagged as likely to persist, indicating an unresolved system issue affecting service delivery
findings.figures: Abandoned vehicles resolution: 97% in Q1, declining to 62% in Q4
findings.quote: The percentage of abandoned vehicles cases resolved within seven days has been steadily declining throughout the whole year from 97% in Q1 to 62% in Q4 due to a delay in a change of the shared system used county wide with Sussex Police and the County Council. The service area has flagged that this slippage may continue to be a challenge in the first half of 2026/27.

findings.headline: The Arc capital project running two years late on water connection with £300k cost overrun funded from contingency
findings.detail: The Arc (Centre for Outdoor Sports) is estimated to overspend by circa £300k. Water utilities work commissioned by Homes England remains ongoing into 2026/27, with South East Water not completing the permanent water connection after a delay of almost two years. A temporary bowser has been put in place to maintain supply. The council is funding the cost overrun from capital programme reserve contingency, with recovery expected from South East Water via Homes England.
findings.matters: Major capital project experiencing significant delivery delays and cost overruns, with recovery dependent on third parties
findings.figures: The Arc estimated overspend circa £300k; water connection delayed almost two years; funded from capital contingency
findings.quote: The Arc is estimated to overspend by circa £300k, reflecting the fact that water utilities work commissioned by Homes England as part of the preliminary groundworks package remains ongoing into 2026/27. South East Water has not yet completed the permanent water connection. That delay has now extended to almost two years.

findings.headline: Housing demand surge with 41% increase in homeless acceptances, managed through reserves with further growth anticipated
findings.detail: Housing demand continues to increase significantly, with 141 households accepted as homeless in Q4, up from 103 in the previous year. Housing Options service redesign created net pressure of £100k, managed through reserves. The council proposes topping up the Homelessness Support Reserve (currently £448k) to support pressures above budget in future years as demand continues to grow.
findings.matters: Demand-led service under significant pressure with council relying on reserves to manage growth; further pressures anticipated and budgets may prove inadequate
findings.figures: 141 homeless households accepted Q4 vs 103 previous year (41% increase); Housing Options in-sourcing created £100k net pressure; Homelessness Support Reserve £448k
findings.quote: Housing demand continues to increase significantly, with 141 households accepted as homeless in Q4, up from 103 in the previous year. Temporary accommodation numbers have risen, alongside increases in households approaching the Council for support, reflecting wider national pressures.

findings.headline: Parking income shortfall and temporary contract costs from EU exit creating revenue pressure
findings.detail: Parking Services has an overspend of £139k due to under-recovery of Penalty Charge Notice (PCN) income plus unforeseen Q4 costs for a temporary contract arrangement put in place following EU exit for fee collection. Permanent procurement is needed urgently to manage further financial pressure.
findings.matters: Parking is an income-generating service with revenue shortfall; council is carrying temporary costs and permanent solution not yet procured
findings.figures: Parking Services £139k overspend; previously unforeseen Q4 temporary contract costs noted
findings.quote: Parking Services: has a net overspend of £139k (breakeven at Q3). This is due to under-recovery of the Penalty Charge Notice (PCN) income. In addition there has been a previously unforeseen cost pressure during Q4 for the temporary contract put in place (a result of EU exit) for the collection of fees.

findings.headline: District Plan examination ongoing with examination costs shifted to 2026/27 and anticipated reserve draws
findings.detail: The District plan examination did not conclude in 2025/26 as anticipated and remains in examination. Costs initially planned for 2025/26 have now shifted to 2026/27. The council anticipates drawing from the reserve to support the examination, which is expected to conclude late 2026. Until then, pressure from speculative development and appeal costs will continue.
findings.matters: Delayed plan adoption affects the council's 5-year housing land supply and extends the period of costly plan-making and appeals activity, consuming reserves that might otherwise be available
findings.figures: Planning directorate £73k underspend, with costs deferred; examination continuing into 2026/27; anticipated reserve draw
findings.quote: the District plan examination did not conclude in 2025/26 as anticipated, and the Plan remains in examination. Therefore, the costs expected in 2025/26 have now shifted to 2026/27. As the examination continues into 2026/27 we anticipate drawing from the reserve to support the examination.

findings.headline: Member interest declarations not maintained to current standards
findings.detail: While the council publishes members' declarations of interest on its website as required, some declarations were not updated by members in a timely manner and were revised only after the auditors flagged this issue during the audit. This represents a governance control weakness.
findings.matters: Lapses in interest declarations governance indicate weak oversight of compliance controls and potential conflicts of interest that have not been adequately managed or disclosed.
findings.figures: Not specified in report
findings.quote: members declarations of interest are required to be accessible and published on the Council's website. The audit found that while the Council does publish these declarations on the website, some were not updated by members in a timely manner and were revised only after this was noted during the audit

findings.headline: Pension asset valuation error of £0.398m not corrected due to immateriality threshold
findings.detail: The auditors identified a judgemental error of £0.398m in the valuation of pension assets arising from timing differences and changes in asset value assumptions after the actuary's initial submission. Management decided not to adjust the accounts because the error was not material to the council's consolidated financial statements, but this represents a control weakness in pension accounting.
findings.matters: Uncorrected valuation errors, even if individually immaterial, can accumulate and erode balance sheet reliability; the error magnitude warrants attention given the council's prior audit disclaimers.
findings.figures: £0.398m judgemental error
findings.quote: We identified a judgemental error of £0.398m, this error arose because after information was submitted to the actuary final adjustments were made to the Pension Fund asset values during the production of the Pension Fund Draft Financial Statements. Since this error was caused by a timing difference and changes in assumptions relating to assets values and was not material to the Council's financial statements management decided not to adjust the accounts for this error

findings.headline: Forecast budget gaps of £1.12m to £1.18m annually from 2026/27 to 2028/29
findings.detail: The Medium-Term Financial Plan projects cumulative deficits: £1.12m in 2026/27, £1.17m in 2027/28, and £1.18m in 2028/29. The council approved a balanced budget for 2025/26 by drawing £0.35m from reserves. However, the council maintains reserves of £41.24m (with unallocated general fund of £14.36m), sufficient to cover these gaps through to 2028/29 within the Local Government Reorganisation timelines.
findings.matters: Persistent multi-year budget gaps indicate structural funding pressures; however, strong reserves provide a buffer. A lender would need to assess whether these gaps reflect sustainable service delivery or if reserves are masking unresolved pressures.
findings.quote: the projections to 2028/29 indicate anticipated budget gaps over the following three financial years: Year 2026/27 is forecast to have a gap of £1.12m, Year 2027/28 a gap of £1.17m, and Year 2028/29 a gap of £1.18m

findings.headline: Material valuation errors corrected in property, plant and equipment
findings.detail: Management changed the valuation method for halls and community centres from Existing Use Value (EUV) to Depreciated Replacement Cost (DRC) but applied it prospectively instead of retrospectively, resulting in a £7.55m opening balance impact and £6.76m effect in 2024/25. Additionally, land was overvalued by £0.07m based on a 2021 offer when current market conditions indicated lower value. Both errors were corrected in the financial statements.
findings.matters: Property valuation errors of this magnitude indicate weaknesses in technical accounting controls and suggest asset values may be overstated; lenders need assurance that tangible asset backing is reliable.
findings.figures: £7.55m opening balance impact, £6.76m in 2024/25, £0.07m land overstatement
findings.quote: management reviewed the valuation methodology for halls and community centres and made a change from Existing Use Value (EUV) to Depreciated Replacement Cost (DRC). However, this change was implemented prospectively instead of retrospectively, as required by the accounting framework. The adjustment in valuation resulted in an impact to the opening balance of £7.55m and £6.76m in 2024/25

findings.headline: Audit opinion qualified due to prior-year disclaimers over property valuation and reserves
findings.detail: The auditors could not gain sufficient audit evidence over the £25.29m valuation of land and buildings last revalued in 2022/23, and over the classification of reserves between useable and unusable categories. This stems from prior disclaimers on 2023/24 and 2022/23 statements. The 2024/25 opinion is therefore modified, and the auditors expect to issue a qualified 'except for' opinion rather than an unqualified one.
findings.matters: A qualified audit opinion signals unresolved control and valuation issues that undermine financial statement reliability; lenders need to know whether balance sheet items are accurately stated.
findings.figures: £25.29m in property, plant and equipment; prior disclaimers on 2022/23 and 2023/24
findings.quote: we did not have sufficient appropriate audit evidence over: The valuation of Land and Buildings included within property, plant and equipment that were last revalued in the financial year 2022/23, amounting to £25.29m

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan and Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: Funding formula disadvantage: Notional Council Tax assumption exceeds actual collectible tax
findings.detail: Under Funding Reform 2.0, the funding formula assumes councils can raise Notional National Council Tax higher than Mid Sussex can actually collect from its resident base. This structural disadvantage reduces council's relative funding allocation and limits ability to grow revenue organically.
findings.matters: Council is penalized by funding formula relative to actual revenue-raising capacity. This is structural, not cyclical, and reduces funding flexibility permanently.
findings.figures: Notional Council Tax (formula assumption) stated as higher than actual collectible Council Tax; current Band D £202.22 post-2.95% rise
findings.quote: the Notional National Council Tax becomes the level the funding formula assumes you can raise in tax, however this is currently higher than that which the Council can raise.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan and Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: Council Tax base growth slowing: 1.57% actual vs 1.6% modelled for future years
findings.detail: Council Tax base grew only 1.57% to 67,847.5 Band D equivalents (30 November 2025), down from 1.66% prior year. Despite this slowdown, council is modelling 1.6% growth for 2027/28 onwards. Slowing property growth reduces organic revenue growth available to offset cost pressures.
findings.matters: Slowing property base growth reduces organic revenue growth. As demographic growth slows, council must rely more on tax rises or service cuts to absorb inflation.
findings.figures: CTB growth 2025: 1.57% (vs 1.66% prior year); modelled growth 2027/28+: 1.6%; Band D equivalents 67,847.5
findings.quote: This year has seen growth of 1.57% (compared to 1.66% at 30 November 2024) which increased the tax base to 67,847.5 Band D equivalents.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan and Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: Loss of £1.236m New Homes Bonus grant in 2026/27 as part of funding settlement consolidation
findings.detail: New Homes Bonus (£1.236m in 2025/26) has been abolished and rolled into general funding formula as part of Funding Reform 2.0. While Revenue Support Grant increased correspondingly, this removes flexibility and discretion from council planning.
findings.matters: Loss of discretionary grant removes flexibility for investment and reserves building. Council has less control over allocation of consolidated funding.
findings.figures: New Homes Bonus 2025/26: £1.236m; ended 2026/27
findings.quote: the end to New Homes Bonus (NHB) for which the Council received £1.236m in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan and Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: Homelessness and temporary accommodation pressures growing; council running acquisition programme with delegated authority
findings.detail: Council explicitly names 'unprecedented levels of homelessness and the pressure on Temporary Accommodation (TA) as serious and debilitating challenges.' Demand rising due to cost-of-living crisis, legislative changes, and shrinking private rental market. Council has set aside match funding for LAHF tranche 3 (additional £800k grant) and delegated authority to procure housing stock.
findings.matters: Homelessness and TA represent uncontrollable cost pressure across local government. This council is explicitly committing capital to housing acquisition, signalling this pressure will continue and absorb increasing resources.
findings.figures: 270+ people attended Homelessness Surgeries past year; £800k additional LAHF grant identified; Capital TA Programme with delegated procurement authority to director
findings.quote: unprecedented levels of homelessness and the pressure on Temporary Accommodation (TA) are serious and debilitating challenges for many of our neighbours.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan and Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (£2.5m for waste service) expected to decline over time
findings.detail: Council receives £2.5m EPR funding in 2025/26, designated to cover costs of Simpler Recycling (1-2-3 waste collection) rollout to 72,000 households. However, council explicitly acknowledges EPR is 'a tax set to change behaviours' and therefore 'returns will diminish over time.' No guarantee on EPR payment levels from 2026/27 onwards. As EPR declines, council must cut waste costs or absorb loss elsewhere.
findings.matters: A material revenue stream (£2.5m, 10.4% of net spending) is explicitly declining. This creates downside income risk and forces either service reduction, cost control, or use of reserves.
findings.figures: EPR funding 2025/26: £2.5m; Simpler Recycling service growth: £1,028k; no guaranteed EPR payment 2026/27+
findings.quote: EPR funding being an allocation of tax, which is levied on producers, is designed to change behaviours. Therefore, it should be expected that returns will diminish over time.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan and Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: From 2027/28, reserves must be drawn down to balance budget—flagged as unsustainable by council
findings.detail: MTFP shows council can balance 2026/27 through treasury income and small reserve contributions (£234k). From 2027/28 onwards, deficits force reserve drawdowns. S151 Officer explicitly states this approach 'is not a sustainable position over the medium term.' General Reserve estimated at £11.9m on 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: Sustained reserve drawdown signals inability to balance operations from recurring revenue. With £11.9m reserves and deficits of £2.1m–£6.4m, reserves would deplete rapidly without intervention.
findings.figures: General Reserve £11.9m (31 March 2027); reserve drawdown begins 2027/28; deficits 2027/28 onwards total £9.5m over three years
findings.quote: However, from 2027/28 the use of Reserves to balance the Budget will be required, this is not a sustainable position over the medium term, and the Council must work to bring this back into balance over the Medium Term Financial Plan period.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Corporate Plan and Budget 2026-2027
findings.headline: Structural deficit of £6.4m by 2029/30, driven by Business Rates funding cliff edge
findings.detail: MTFP projects balanced budget 2026/27, then deficits of £949k (2027/28), £2.1m (2028/29), and £6.4m (2029/30). Council identifies a £6m funding gap by end of three-year settlement, caused by Funding Reform 2.0 and Business Rates Retention reset. S151 Officer notes this cliff edge must be managed while sustainable plans are developed.
findings.matters: A £6.4m structural deficit in year four represents fundamental sustainability challenge requiring major service reductions or borrowing. This directly impacts debt service capacity and financial viability.
findings.figures: 2029/30 deficit £6,444k; 2028/29 deficit £2,090k; identified funding gap almost £6m by end of settlement
findings.quote: Current models show a deficit of circa £6m by the end of the multi-year settlement, based on the governments assessment of funding need via the formula.

findings.headline: Council proposes extending maximum investment period with other local authorities from 1 year to 2 years
findings.detail: Council seeks to extend the maximum maturity of local authority investments from 1 year to 2 years. The council notes it previously restricted LA lending duration 'to reduce the duration of investments with other Local Authorities' due to intervention concerns. The extension is justified as a trade-off to secure higher yields, as 'many local authorities will pay rates considerably higher than bank or building society rates'.
findings.matters: Lengthening investment maturity with stressed counterparties reduces flexibility if a council requires intervention or faces difficulty. Longer duration commitments reduce the council's ability to exit or reallocate if circumstances change.
findings.figures: Extension from 1-year to 2-year maximum maturity; local authority lending limit £5m per counterparty
findings.quote: This authority resolved not to invest in other Local Authorities where there was any Government intervention and at the same time to reduce the duration of investments with other Local Authorities to 1 year. It is proposed that this is increased to 2 years. Whilst borrowing rates remain high, many local authorities will pay rates considerably higher than bank or building society rates in order to secure borrowing.

findings.headline: Council concentrated 56% of investment portfolio (£53m) in lending to other local authorities, up from 29% in six months
findings.detail: Investment composition shifted dramatically towards concentrated local authority lending. LA investments rose from £23m (29% of portfolio) at 31 March 2025 to £53m (56% of £94.6m portfolio) at 30 September 2025, while bank deposits fell from 14% to 4%. This represents a material shift toward correlated counterparty risk at a time when councils nationally face fiscal pressures.
findings.matters: Concentrating cash reserves with other councils creates correlated credit risk. If stressed councils experience difficulty or require intervention, the council's liquidity could be at risk. Many English councils face pressure from central government funding cuts and rising costs.
findings.figures: Local authorities £53m (56% of total £94.583m) at 30 Sept 2025, up from £23m (29% of £79.815m) at 31 Mar 2025; banks fell from £11.36m (14%) to £3.09m (4%)
findings.quote: Table 4 Treasury Investments Local authorities: 31.03.2025 23.000 [£m] 29%, 30.09.2025 53.000 [£m] 56%

findings.headline: Capital expenditure projected to fall 62% from £14.5m to £5.5m in 2026/27, with capital receipts dropping to zero
findings.detail: Capital spending plans show a dramatic contraction from £14.531m in 2025/26 to £5.515m in 2026/27. Capital receipts (asset sales) of £5.7m in 2025/26 are projected to fall to zero in 2026/27, then capital grants also decline sharply. This suggests a major asset disposal programme is ending and capital investment capacity is materially constrained.
findings.matters: Lenders assess capital investment as a measure of asset maintenance and infrastructure condition. A 62% spending cut signals either completion of an asset disposal programme or severely constrained reinvestment capacity, both material to financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 2025/26 capital expenditure £14.531m, 2026/27 £5.515m (62% reduction); capital receipts £5.7m (2025/26) to £0.000m (2026/27)
findings.quote: Table 1 Capital Expenditure £m General Fund: 2025/26 Estimate 14.531, 2026/27 Estimate 5.515. Table 2 Capital receipts: 2025/26 Estimate 5.700, 2026/27 Estimate 0.000

findings.headline: Government grants and S106 contributions fund 47% of the five-year capital programme, creating significant external funding dependency.
findings.detail: Of the £24,463k capital programme 2026–2030, £11,603k comes from government grants and S106 contributions. Capital receipts fund £5,586k, Capital Reserve £2,411k, and specific reserves £1,037k. The funding structure makes the capital programme vulnerable to changes in government priorities or reductions in grant awards.
findings.matters: High dependency on external grant and developer contribution funding exposes capital investment plans to decisions outside council control; loss or reprioritisation of grants would force programme contraction.
findings.figures: Total programme £24,463k: Grants/Contributions £11,603k (47%), Capital Receipts £5,586k (23%), Capital Reserve £2,411k (10%), Specific Reserves £1,037k (4%).
findings.quote: Grants/Contributions – specific grants from Central Government and Contributions from third parties that are provided to deliver specific schemes i.e. DEFRA grant to partially fund the introduction of Simpler Recycling, the Local Authority Housing Fund and Disabled Facilities Grant.

findings.headline: Council policy explicitly prohibits external borrowing and restricts all capital to pre-identified funding sources.
findings.detail: The strategy states 'the Council's policy is that no external borrowing will be undertaken and that all capital schemes will only be undertaken when specific funding has been identified, i.e., capital receipts, Government grants, S106 payments, or other identified contributions.' This self-imposed constraint limits the council's ability to respond to capital needs without identified pre-funding.
findings.matters: A rigid no-borrowing policy constrains flexibility to respond to unforeseen capital needs or opportunities, creating dependency on external funding timing.
findings.figures: Policy applies to all capital schemes across the £24,463k five-year programme.
findings.quote: Although the Council's policy is that no external borrowing will be undertaken and that all capital schemes will only be undertaken when specific funding has been identified, i.e., capital receipts, Government grants, S106 payments, or other identified contributions

findings.headline: Council established dedicated Capital Reserve in 2024/25 specifically to reduce general fund pressure on capital investment.
findings.detail: The strategy explains that 'a Capital Reserve was created to reduce the need to call on the general fund resources for capital projects, and to ring fence non-specific funds agreed to fund projects.' The council is drawing £2.4m from this reserve in the current capital programme. Creating a separate reserve specifically to relieve general fund pressure indicates the council was struggling to fund capital from existing revenue resources.
findings.matters: Reserve creation to ease general fund pressure is a symptom of underlying budget stress and constraint on revenue flexibility.
findings.figures: Capital Reserve contribution: £2,411k of £24,463k total capital programme; reserve created in 2024/25.
findings.quote: In 2024/25 a Capital Reserve was created to reduce the need to call on the general fund resources for capital projects, and to ring fence non-specific funds agreed to fund projects.
